This read is built on just 28.3 innings from a prior season, and the sample is too thin to lock in confidence about whether the swing-and-miss tool can stick in a structured MLB environment.

700255_pitcher.text: Jacob Steinmetz is a 22-year-old A+ pitcher showing modest strikeout production (8.4 K/9) paired with concerning walk rates (3.9 BB/9) in his 57.7 innings this season. His K-BB% sits at 11.1%—well below league average and placing him in the 41st percentile among comparable pitchers—while a 4.37 ERA reflects overall inconsistency. The core risk is control: even when translated to MLB equivalents, his 4.0 BB/9 sits above league average, suggesting he lacks the precision to elevate from a multi-inning relief profile. This is a prior-season sample with high staleness risk, and confidence in any projection is low.

700280_pitcher.text: Miguel Mendez is a right-handed starter operating as a back-of-the-rotation depth arm with middling command and strikeout rates in limited AA work. His K/9 of 9.9 and K-BB% of 13.7% both sit around the 55th percentile against the pitcher pool, but a 4.4 BB/9 and 4.93 ERA signal he cannot yet consistently execute in the zone at this level. The core risk is thin current sample—just 34.7 IP—which limits confidence in whether these rates represent true performance or noise before he compiles meaningful upper-level innings.

700283_hitter.text: Derlin Figueroa is a high-leverage power hitter whose A+ line—.582 slugging, .298 ISO—sits at the 97th percentile for bat speed and hard contact, but the 27.2% strikeout rate signals a hitter who is chasing and missing at a clip well above MLB average (22.0%). The walk rate of 12.1% (MLB-equivalent: 9.3%) keeps his on-base game respectable, though the strikeout volume will constrain his upside if he doesn't tighten his zone discipline. This is a 224 PA active sample with no staleness, so the power is real—the question is whether a 22-year-old at A+ can lower the whiffs enough to get enough contact to matter in the majors.

700321_hitter.text: Andy Perez is a left-handed hitter with an elite batting average (.312) and contact rate (13.1 K%) that translates to strong pitch recognition at the plate, but his power output is a significant concern—an ISO of .092 sits in the 17th percentile and projects to just .104 in the majors, well below the league average of .15. His walk rate of 3.7% is also critically weak (1st percentile), leaving little margin for error when balls in play don't fall. The 267 PA sample is current and clean, though the profile reads as a speed-or-position-dependent prospect rather than a hitter-first asset.

700327_pitcher.text: Welinton Herrera is a high-velocity left-hander who misses bats at an elite rate—94th percentile K/9 at 13.5 per 9—but operates with loose control that undercuts the strikeout advantage, posting a 5.6 BB/9 (31st percentile). The 5.16 ERA and 1.72 WHIP over 22.7 IP in AAA reflect a pitcher who can blow fastballs past hitters but consistently falls behind in counts, and elbow inflammation has landed him on the 60-day IL, creating immediate availability risk. The sample is fresh but thin, and the injury is a hard ceiling on any near-term impact.

700400_pitcher.text: Matt Ager is a right-handed depth arm whose feel for command outpaces his ability to generate whiffs—a pitcher more likely to eat innings than dominate from an MLB mound. His 3.2 BB/9 ranks 82nd percentile in the pitcher pool, but his 7.5 K/9 (13th percentile) and 10.9 K-BB% (41st percentile) reveal limited margin for error; translated to MLB context, he'd sit around 7.9 K/9 and 3.3 BB/9, barely above the league average walk rate. The 4.5 ERA and 1.47 WHIP across 36 IP at AA reflect modest run prevention, and without substantial miss-rate improvement, he's likely capped as a useful depth option rather than a rotation contributor. The current sample is fresh but modest in size, so the floor-to-upside range remains wide.

700731_hitter.text: Keiner Delgado is a contact-heavy, patient hitter whose plate discipline (87th percentile BB%, 89th percentile K%) forms his only clear above-average tool, but he lacks the bat speed or gap power to generate consistent impact—his .118 ISO projects well below league average and sits at just the 35th percentile. The translation from AAA shows 20.0% K against 11.6% BB in an MLB equivalent, a ratio that demands him to hit for average just to reach replaceable utility value. His current AAA sample is thin (56 PA), and ValuCast's rankings have cooled on him by 71 spots in three days, reflecting skepticism about whether approach alone sustains a professional career.

700924_pitcher.text: The strikeout rate translates to big-league average, which is the only good news in this profile. At AA, Mozzicato is posting an 8.8 BB/9 and a 2.1 WHIP, and those figures move to a 6.4 BB/9 equivalent against MLB hitters, roughly double what a league-average arm allows. He is missing bats, 11.0 K/9 at the level, 58 strikeouts in 47.3 innings, but the command has collapsed so completely that the whipping motion through the zone doesn't matter much when he can't find it consistently enough to string outs together. This profile hinges entirely on whether the walk rate comes down; if it doesn't, the ceiling of a depth or relief arm becomes the floor too.

700932_hitter.text: Kyle Manzardo is a power-contact tradeoff hitter built on strong barrel control but hamstrung by a 31.8% strikeout rate that sits in the bottom 7th percentile. His Statcast profile shows elite barrel rate (75th percentile at 11.6%) and excellent plate discipline on walks (70th percentile at 10.7%), yet his xBA of .227 ranks just 20th percentile—he makes hard contact when he connects, but connects infrequently. The ValuCast projection of .230 AVG / .407 SLG reflects that gap: 20 home runs in 530 PA is realistic given the power floor, but the strikeouts and low contact rate will keep him from reaching his xwOBA ceiling of .315. Medium confidence reflects the volatility between his elite tooling and his severe swing-and-miss issue.

700933_pitcher.text: Chris Cortez is a right-handed pitcher generating swing-and-miss stuff (11.7 K/9 across 15.3 IP at AA) but fighting serious command issues that have inflated his ERA to 4.7 with a 1.96 WHIP. His 8.8 BB/9 is the primary constraint—translated to the MLB equivalent, that projects to 7.2 BB/9, well above league average and a structural ceiling on his value. This is a thin sample at an early stage, so the command profile may sharpen with additional reps, but right now he profiles as a depth arm or bullpen option rather than a starting path.

701056_pitcher.text: Josh Grosz is a bat-missing righthander running elite strikeout rates at AA—13.2 K/9 (92nd percentile)—but his walk rate of 5.1 BB/9 and 1.37 WHIP signal he hasn't yet earned command consistency at the upper minors. The MLB-equivalent translation projects a 4.1 BB/9 and 9.4 K/9, meaningful improvements but still above-average risk on the control axis. With only 30 innings in this sample, confidence is low; the strikeout profile is real, but the command floor remains unproven.

701178_pitcher.text: Rafe Schlesinger is a left-hander generating swing-and-miss at a high rate—89th percentile K/9 at 12.0 K/9 (minor-league line)—but control has deteriorated sharply in his AA debut, posting an 8.64 ERA over just 8.3 innings with a 3.2 BB/9. His A+ sample of 45 IP shows the profile more clearly: 12.6 K/9 with better command (3.6 BB/9) and a 22.2% K-BB%, but a 1.51 WHIP and 4.4 ERA suggest the strikeouts haven't translated to dominance. The immediate risk is real control trouble at the new level; the current sample is too thin to confirm whether this is early-season noise or a meaningful step-down in execution.

701327_hitter.text: Elijah Green is a high-strikeout prospect who shows enough power to project as a reserve but struggles sharply with contact—45.5% K% in A+ play ranks in the 1st percentile against the ValuCast hitter pool. His .172 ISO (65th percentile) and 10.9% BB% suggest he can hit for some damage when he connects, but a .204 AVG and .292 OBP across 257 plate appearances demonstrate he is not connecting enough to stay playable at present rates. The translation to MLB equivalents projects 41.6% K% and .131 ISO, well below average, which compounds the contact problem—this is a swing-and-miss profile without the power floor to absorb the whiffs. With the sample current and live, confidence in the overall arc depends on whether Green can demonstrate material improvement in contact rates; right now the risk is skewed heavily toward continued strikeout dominance over value creation.

701328_pitcher.text: A 7.00 ERA at AAA is hard to dress up, and the walk rate is the reason. Across 53 innings he's running 5.6 BB/9, which translates to 4.6 at the MLB level while the MLB average sits at 3.2, a gap wide enough to explain everything else. The strikeout rate doesn't compensate; his translated K/9 lands at 7.9, below the MLB mean, leaving a K-BB% of 9.2% when the league runs 13.5%. If the command doesn't develop, there's a depth arm here at best, and even that hinges on finding some margin between the strikeouts and the free passes, because right now that margin is thin enough to make the floor feel closer than the ceiling.

701337_hitter.text: Ethan Petry is a power-first hitter showing elite-percentile ISO and OPS against AA competition but struggling badly with plate discipline in his brief exposure at that level. Over 37 PA at AA, he's struck out at 37.8% while walking just 5.4%, and his .206 AVG reflects contact failure rather than a power problem—the 22-year-old's .500 SLG suggests he's still barreling the ball when he makes contact. His A+ track record (.297/.392/.521 over 194 PA, 86th percentile ISO) shows a more functional approach, but the current strikeout rate and BB% collapse signal he's not yet ready to exploit his power at AA. This is a thin sample in real time, so the read leans on how sharply his discipline has degraded on the promotion.

701339_hitter.text: The .315 average is the loudest thing on this card, and the 95th-percentile hit tool grade against his minor-league peers backs up why it isn't just noise from a .379 BABIP propping everything up. Twenty-eight stolen bases out of a 309-PA sample at AA tells you the profile has dimension, and a 12% walk rate at the level translates to a still-above-average 9.2% equivalent at MLB, which keeps the .394 OBP from being a mirage. The power is the ceiling limiter: his ISO equivalent at the big-league level comes out to .109 against a major-league norm of .150, and until that gap closes, Houston profiles as a bench or platoon shortstop rather than a regular, with the hit tool and legs doing all the carrying.

701364_pitcher.text: The walk rate is the argument here, full stop. Arnold is running 4.3 BB/9 at AA, and when you translate that to an MLB context it climbs to 4.2 against a league baseline closer to 3.2, so the command problem doesn't soften with level adjustment. His K/9 at 9.5 in the minors lands at just 8.1 equivalent, below average, which means there's no strikeout upside waiting to paper over the control. If he tightens the zone and the walks come down, there's a back-end starter here with innings-eating volume already in evidence across 80.3 IP as a 22-year-old. If the walks don't move, the floor is a depth arm.

701388_pitcher.text: The strikeouts are loud and the walks are a problem. Cijntje's 11.1 K/9 at AA translates to a near-league-average 8.9 at the MLB level, which is a usable miss tool, but his 4.7 BB/9 translates to 4.4 against a major-league average closer to 3.2, and that gap is what's dragging his K-BB% below where it needs to be for a back-end starter to survive. The skill-shape grades tell the same story: a 60 on miss, a 35 on command, those two numbers pointed in opposite directions across 74.3 innings of AA work. If the command closes even partially, there's a back-end starter here with a projected 70% chance at a starter or late-inning role; if it doesn't, this becomes a depth arm with a good strikeout pitch and nowhere to put it.

701392_hitter.text: The .396 OBP and 16% walk rate at A+ are the loudest signals here, but the power backs them up — .231 ISO with 11 home runs in 225 plate appearances is a real volume at this level, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts his walk rate at 10.8%, a step above a league that draws at 8.5%. The K% translates to 24.2% against major-league competition, which isn't clean, so the profile hinges on whether the swing decisions that produce the walks also suppress strikeout escalation as pitching quality rises. If that discipline travels, Dinges profiles as a patient, impact bat who can occupy a lineup spot; if it doesn't, the DH-only profile leaves him without a defensive fallback, and a bench role is more likely than a regular job.

701394_hitter.text: .388 OBP out of Triple-A, and the walk rate translates to 11.6% against a major-league average of 8.5% — the approach isn't a minor-league mirage. Ehrhard's raw ISO sits at .202 in AAA, which the translation compresses to .158 at the MLB level, right around league average, so the power projection is real enough to matter without being the reason to believe in him. The hit tool, the patience, and 11 steals in 369 PA suggest a center fielder who doesn't need to be propped up by one tool. If the contact holds at the highest level, he profiles as a low-end everyday regular; if it doesn't, he's a useful bench piece with genuine on-base value.

701398_hitter.text: The barrel rate tells the story here: 14.8% puts Stewart in the 91st percentile, and his .469 xSLG reflects a hitter who makes genuinely hard contact when he squares one up. The gap between that xSLG and his xBA at .249 is the whole tension in the profile — he barrels at an elite clip but whiffs at 27.5%, which bleeds enough contact quality to keep the batting average ordinary. At 11.3% walks he controls the zone well enough to prop up the on-base side, and the projection lands on .800 OPS with 30 home runs over a full season, which is a useful corner bat even if the batting average never stretches past league average. The profile holds as long as the barrel rate isn't a small-sample gift; the 27.5% whiff rate suggests pitchers will keep testing him, and if he can't improve his contact rate, the power plays but the average sinks and he becomes a low-.250s slugger who lives on walks and damage.

701411_pitcher.text: The walk rate is the story here. A 2.3 BB/9 across 68 innings between A+ and AA translates to a projected 2.8 at the MLB level, below a league average that sits at 3.2, and the 93rd-percentile command grade reflects that shape cleanly. The strikeout rate is fine, not loud, and the translation to 8.4 K/9 against a major-league average of 8.6 confirms he's working the edges of competence rather than missing bats at volume. What makes this profile function is the combination: a K-BB% that translates to 14.2% against a 13.5% baseline means the walks he doesn't issue are doing real work, covering for strikeout stuff that won't carry a full rotation. The ceiling, honestly, is a useful arm, somewhere between a fifth starter and a reliable middle-relief option, and it hinges entirely on whether that command holds once opposing hitters have quality looks at his stuff.

701480_pitcher.text: The ERA sits at 4.2 and the WHIP at 1.30, which are the two numbers doing the most flattering work in this profile, because everything underneath them tells a harder story. At A+, the walk rate is 4.8 per nine, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts that at 4.4 when the big-league average sits at 3.2 — command is the problem, not an outlier game or two. The strikeout rate doesn't offset it: 8.4 per nine at the level translates to 7.5 equivalent, below the major-league mean, which leaves a K-BB% that grades 35 across the board on miss, command, and dominance. Run prevention grading at 55 is essentially the ERA and WHIP papering over the underlying shape, and the honest version of this profile is a depth arm who gets out of trouble more than his stuff says he should. If the walks follow him up the ladder, there's nothing left to hide behind; if they don't, a useful MLB arm is the ceiling worth holding for.

701481_hitter.text: A .404 OBP at Double-A from a catcher is the kind of number that makes you stop scrolling. Ryan Campos is walking at 15% in the AA line, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts his walk rate well above the big-league norm, which tells you the approach grade in the projection isn't flattery. The ISO translates to .146 MLB-equivalent, right at the major-league average, so the bat works because the strike zone command is genuine, not because balls are flying out. If he hits enough to stick behind the plate, he profiles as a bench-or-platoon piece with a low-end regular ceiling; if the .355 BABIP drifts and the strikeouts tick up at Triple-A, what's left is a reserve floor.

701527_hitter.text: A .477 OBP at AA, with 74 walks against 60 strikeouts in 354 plate appearances, is not a profile you usually see outside the top hundred names in the system. The translated walk rate lands at 14.5% against a major-league average of 8.5%, and the power projects at .167 ISO in the show, which is modest but real given the hit-tool grade driving the top line. The whole argument hinges on whether a .409 BABIP softens as the level rises, because if his hit tool grades out closer to a 55 than a 65, the ceiling compresses and you're looking at a bench piece with a good eye rather than an everyday center fielder. Everything else in the shape says everyday regular is the right call.

701538_hitter.text: The xwOBA sits at .302 and the xBA at .238, and that gap is the whole profile: he makes loud contact when he connects, but a 35.6% chase rate keeps him from connecting often enough. The 44.5% hard-hit rate is genuine, and 29.0 ft/s sprint speed adds a dimension that shows up in the projected 27 steals, but the plate discipline is the ceiling cap, not a fixable footnote. If the chase rate doesn't move, you're looking at a second-division regular who helps in speed and sneaks you 19 home runs, which at 22 in a full-time San Diego outfield job is a useful floor, not a disappointment.

701542_pitcher.text: The fastball spin is the one elite trait holding this profile together: 2540 rpm sits at the 91st percentile, and that's doing real work against a 22.9% strikeout rate that's essentially league average and a 22.2% whiff rate that ranks in the bottom third of starters. The control is the one thing that keeps him from slipping backward, a 7.6% walk rate that grades well above most of his peers, but the xERA at 4.25 and a hard-hit rate of 39.9% say the underlying margin is thin. Warren looks like a back-of-the-rotation regular who can eat starts and protect a lead long enough to hand it off. If the spin doesn't translate to swings-and-misses at a higher rate as hitters see him more, what's left is a durable arm with a nice walk rate and not much else to force decisions.

701590_pitcher.text: The ERA sits at 3.40 over 55 AA innings, which looks better than the stuff underneath it. Translated to MLB context, his strikeout rate drops to 7.5 per nine while his walk rate comes in at 3.7, and the K-BB% lands at 10.6% where the league norm runs 13.5%. The command grades out average, run prevention grades above it, and the whiff generation grades well below both, a shape that tends to survive in a starter's workload only until hitters get comfortable. If the stuff plays up shortened to relief innings, a multi-inning or setup role is the realistic ceiling, and ValuCast sees 68% odds of a useful MLB arm; if it doesn't, the floor is organizational depth.

701616_hitter.text: Twelve home runs in 235 AA plate appearances from a catcher is not a quiet number, and the .260 ISO backs the shape of it — at the MLB-equivalent level, the raw power translates to a .176 ISO while the league sits at .150. What complicates the profile is everything around the bat: his 10% BB% compresses to 8.6% in translation, barely above the 8.5% MLB average, and the approach grade sits at 45. The BABIP at .262 is doing no favors to a .245 average, so the hit tool carries genuine uncertainty, but if the power holds at a catcher-eligible profile, a low-end everyday regular is the ceiling and a reserve is the floor, with the position doing meaningful work in that gap. The outcome hinges almost entirely on whether the contact can get average enough to let the thump play.

701649_hitter.text: The contact rate is the whole argument. Triantos is hitting .307 in 343 AAA plate appearances with a 13% strikeout rate, and when that number translates to an MLB context it projects to 16.8%, well below what most big leaguers post. That's a legitimately rare skill, and his AAA percentile confirms it: 96th among qualified hitters in K%. The catch is that the walk rate sits at 5%, projecting to 5.9% in MLB context where the average is 8.5%, and the ISO of .120 in translation doesn't clear the league mean, so the whole profile depends on whether that contact quality holds up against better velocity and sharper secondary stuff at the next level. If it does, you're looking at a regular; if the approach doesn't develop, the power ceiling keeps him a bench or platoon piece with a very useful bat.

701656_pitcher.text: The 0.90 ERA across 20.7 AAA innings is loud, and the strikeout shape behind it is genuinely striking, 14.4 K/9 that translates to a still-above-average 9.8 in MLB context, but Henderson is currently on the injured list and this sample is four starts thin. The walk rate is the friction: 4.3 BB/9 at the level softens to 3.6 in translation, a shade above the MLB mean, and the command grade here is a 40. If the stuff plays and the walks tighten, there's a useful MLB arm in the profile; if they don't, this is a depth/relief ceiling and nothing more.

701679_pitcher.text: Brody Brecht is a high-strikeout arm still hunting for command; 13.5 K/9 ranks 94th percentile in the ValuCast pitcher pool, but a 6.5 BB/9 and 1.4 WHIP reflect a starter who is not yet locating consistently enough to grade as reliable. The K-BB% of 17.8% sits at 77th percentile, which shows upside, but the 5.23 ERA translates to a walk rate the system projects as MLB-average or slightly worse (4.6 BB/9 equivalent). This is a depth profile with significant development risk—only 20.7 innings in the current sample, and low confidence in the translation given thin workload.

701680_pitcher.text: RJ Sales is a right-handed depth arm still assembling the stuff to miss bats consistently—he struck out 9.5 per 9 in 94.7 IP at A-ball last season, but that translates to just 7.1 K/9 at the MLB level, well below league average. Command grades as a relative strength (2.7 BB/9, 90th percentile), though control doesn't overcome insufficient strikeout ability. The core risk is modest miss and run prevention (ERA 2.85 in a thin, prior-season sample from June), leaving him ceiling'd as organizational depth rather than a rotation contributor over the next two to three years. ValuCast is rising on him (+14.6 points in three days), but the sample is stale and the strikeout profile remains the primary constraint.

701717_pitcher.text: The ERA and WHIP sit at the 91st percentile among minor-league pitchers this year, which sounds like a star until you look at what's actually generating those results. Across 65.6 IP at AA and A+, the strikeout rate translates to 8.0 K/9 at the MLB level, right where league average lives, and the K-BB% comes in at 12.9% versus a 13.5% MLB average, meaning the run prevention is outrunning the stuff. Command grades as a legitimate asset at 55, and the 2.7 BB/9 in the minors is genuinely clean, but pitchers who don't miss bats tend to find the margins tighter at full speed. If the ERA holds because the contact suppression is durable and the command stays this sharp, he's a useful MLB arm, the outcome the projection leans on heavily at 85%. If it doesn't, what remains is a depth lefty who throws strikes.

701750_hitter.text: Bennett Thompson is a high-contact, high-walk hitter running a 99th-percentile approach at A+, getting on base at elite rates (.495 OBP) with surprising pop (.536 SLG, .222 ISO). His 25.7% walk rate and 17.1% strikeout rate anchor a disciplined profile that translates to a projected 14.9% BB% and 21.7% K% in MLB context. The main risk is that power plays down sharply in translation—from .222 ISO to .150 MLB-equivalent—and catcher depth of role limits ceiling, leaving this as a bench or platoon outcome even if the bat stays intact. The 210 PA sample is current and clean, but early in the season.

701762_hitter.text: The contact rate is the one jagged edge in an otherwise elite profile. Kurtz's 58.3% hard-hit rate and 18.4% walk rate are both genuinely rare, and the .379 xwOBA reflects a hitter who does serious damage when he connects. The problem is a 36.8% whiff rate that sits near the bottom of the league, and whether those two things can coexist at scale is the whole argument. The projection says they can, landing at .263/.394/.505 with 36 projected home runs, essentially betting that the walk rate and raw power are loud enough to carry the strikeouts — and the xSLG of .493 suggests the batted-ball shape backs that up. If the whiff rate doesn't soften as he sees more big-league looks, the average erodes and the profile slides from star to streaky slugger; if it does, you have a middle-of-the-order first baseman with an uncommon combination of patience and thump.

701771_hitter.text: Nineteen home runs in 303 AA plate appearances is the loudest thing about Billy Amick, and the translation backs the thump: his ISO converts to .186 at the MLB level, meaningfully above the .15 MLB baseline. The problem riding alongside it is a 30% strikeout rate that translates to 29.5% in the majors, a figure that puts his .203 average and .221 BABIP in uncomfortable company. His walk rate gives him a floor, translating to 10.4% where the MLB average sits at 8.5%, but if the contact rate doesn't tighten, the hit tool stays a 45 and the power has nobody to carry it. Bench bat with platoon upside is the honest destination here, and it hinges entirely on whether he can make enough contact against better arms to let the plus raw power show up in real games.

701778_hitter.text: The .274 ISO at AA is the whole argument: 16 home runs in 278 plate appearances from a 23-year-old center fielder, with a slugging percentage that translates to .184 ISO against an MLB average around .150. The power grades out at a 75, and it's sitting on a legitimate sample. What it isn't is a disciplined approach — the 29% strikeout rate in Double-A carries to roughly 28.5% in MLB equivalent context, well above the 22% league baseline, and a 40-grade approach puts a hard ceiling on how often he actually gets to use that bat. If the hit tool plays up and he makes enough contact to stay in a lineup, he's a low-end regular with real pop; if the strikeouts don't compress, there's a bench bat with loud days.

701780_pitcher.text: Tanner McDougal is a right-handed starter showing promising strike-to-walk ratios—a 3.75 K-BB% on 10.1 K/9 and 4.9 BB/9 at AAA—but he's working through just 24 innings, making any durability or consistency read speculative at best. The ERA (3.00) and WHIP (1.04) rank well percentile-wise, yet control volatility (walk rate at 44th percentile) and the thin, current workload create real noise in the signal. Given the 24-inning sample size and low confidence in translation, treat this as a depth prospect with significant remain-to-be-proven markers rather than a settled performer.

701785_hitter.text: The .492 slugging at Triple-A is the loudest number, and it translates: the MLB-equivalent ISO comes out at .165, a tick above what a league-average bat produces. Culpepper is hitting .272/.376/.492 over 295 AAA plate appearances with 15 steals and a K% that actually improves when you run it through the translation, dropping to 20.0% where the MLB average sits at 22.0%. If the bat carries to the majors, he's an everyday shortstop at 23; if the level exposes him, the approach and speed leave a real bench bat behind. The one dependency is whether the contact quality sustains, because a .289 BABIP isn't inflated, but it does need to hold.

701795_pitcher.text: The walk rate is the one thing working here, and even that barely clears the bar at the MLB level. Drew Beam has posted a 3.0 BB/9 at AA, genuine command graded 60, but the strikeout rate translates to a 7.0 K/9 while the MLB average sits at 8.6, and his translated K-BB% lands at 10.0 where the league average is 13.5. The ERA at 6.2 over 77 innings is not a small-sample blip; it is the run prevention grade telling you what happens when you miss bats at a 9th-percentile clip and depend entirely on contact suppression that isn't there. If the command holds and something generates whiffs he doesn't currently own, there is a back-end rotation arm buried in the profile; if it doesn't, this is a depth piece who fills innings.

701807_hitter.text: The .292 xBA sitting at the 94th percentile is the loudest number in the profile, and it doesn't come from elite raw contact — his 89.5 mph average exit velocity is right around the middle of the league. What's carrying it is a 27.0% chase rate and a 20.9% whiff rate, both well above average, paired with 28.6 ft/s sprint speed that turns soft contact into problems for defenses. The projection at .263/.328/.409 looks conservative against a .354 xwOBA and .458 xSLG, but the 7.5% walk rate is genuinely thin, and if pitchers learn to work him down in the zone and shrink the zone further, that contact quality softens fast. If the plate discipline holds, he profiles as a solid everyday outfielder with a useful speed-power blend, and 17 home runs and 19 steals in a full season is a real contributor, not a corner piece you're managing around.

701852_hitter.text: The .449 OBP headlining a .998 OPS across 227 combined PA is the loudest thing in the file, and it sits at the 99th percentile against the hitter pool. The BABIP is .401, which matters: the MLB-equivalent translation has his walk rate at 11.4% against a big-league average of 8.5%, and his ISO translates to .17, so the underlying plate discipline and raw power survive the level jump even if the batting average softens considerably. The whole profile hinges on whether a catcher can get enough defensive reps at the MLB level to stay in the lineup, because the translated strikeout rate of 24.5% isn't comfortable for a backup and there's an 85% bench/platoon probability baked into the ceiling already. If the hit tool and approach hold, he's a low-end everyday regular; if that BABIP normalizes and the K rate creeps up without the position giving him margin for error, you've got a roster filler with an interesting spring.
